header: Universal design as a framework for enhancing tourist friendly and well being oriented urban spaces in Luxor Egypt | Discover Cities | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Discover Cities Article Universal design as a framework for enhancing tourist friendly and well being oriented urban spaces in Luxor Egypt Research Open access Published: 07 November 2026 Volume 3 , article number 225 ( 2026 ) Cite this article You have full access to this open access article Download PDF Save article View saved research Discover Cities Aims and scope Submit manuscript Universal design as a framework for enhancing tourist friendly and well being oriented urban spaces in Luxor Egypt Download PDF Menna Allah Salah Refai ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-4496-4763 1 & Zienab El-gamily 2 Abstract Urban spaces in heritage tourist cities play a central role in shaping visitors’ experience and supporting residents’ quality of life. In Luxor, Egypt, the performance of these spaces is strongly influenced by accessibility, environmental comfort, safety, and cultural legibility. This study investigates universal design as an integrative framework to enhance urban well-being and improve tourist experiences in heritage urban environments. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining a systematic literature review, analysis of international best practices, and empirical fieldwork. Primary data were collected through questionnaire surveys administered to 339 participants (55% visitors, 40% residents, 5% professionals) across two key urban areas: Railway Station Square and the surroundings of Luxor Temple, using a five-point Likert scale. Descriptive statistical analysis was applied to the survey data, including frequency distributions and mean score calculations. Independent-samples t-tests were used to compare perceptions between residents and tourists. Observational data were interpreted using universal design indicators. The findings reveal significant deficiencies: approximately 95% of respondents confirmed the lack of accessible infrastructure for all users, 88.2% reported the absence of adequate seating and shading, and approximately 82.4% considered street surfaces unsafe for movement. These deficiencies negatively influence perceived comfort, ease of movement, and overall user satisfaction. This study concludes that integrating universal design principles into heritage urban planning can substantially improve urban well-being and enhance the quality of the tourist experience, while supporting inclusive and sustainable development in culturally sensitive cities. Highlights Universal design improves accessibility and perceived urban well-being in heritage tourist cities. Empirical assessment of public spaces in Luxor reveals critical accessibility and comfort gaps. Findings support integrating inclusive design principles into heritage urban development strategies. header: Spatiotemporal dynamics of informal settlement thermal environments and their driving factors in Nairobi, Kenya | Discover Cities | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Discover Cities Article Spatiotemporal dynamics of informal settlement thermal environments and their driving factors in Nairobi, Kenya Research Open access Published: 07 November 2026 Volume 3 , article number 224 ( 2026 ) Cite this article You have full access to this open access article Download PDF Save article View saved research Discover Cities Aims and scope Submit manuscript Spatiotemporal dynamics of informal settlement thermal environments and their driving factors in Nairobi, Kenya Download PDF Godfrey Nkugwa 1 & Doreen Loyo 1 Abstract Rapid urbanization in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) has expanded informal settlements where residents face extreme heat, yet informal settlement thermal dynamics remain understudied. Nowhere is this more evident than in Nairobi, one of SSA’s most rapidly growing metropolises, which faces critical challenges from unregulated informal settlement expansion, characterized by high population density and threats to urban sustainability and resident well-being. Using Landsat 8/9 imagery from three February scenes (2015, 2020, 2025), remotely sensed indices, and geospatial data, this study investigated land surface temperature (LST) evolution across Nairobi’s 17 subdivisions and 13 mapped informal settlements, of which 12 were retained for formal analysis. Informal settlements consistently exhibited elevated LSTs, with Kibera approximately 2.6 °C warmer than its parent administrative subdivision in 2015 (34.28 °C vs. 31.67 °C), a pattern that persisted with variations of 1.5–2.9 °C. The urban heat island followed a persistent east–west gradient: industrial and informal settlements were > 95% heat-dominated, while western highlands remained cool. The anomalously wet February of 2020 temporarily reduced area-weighted mean LST from 33.1 °C (2015) to 29.9 °C (2020), with partial rebound to 30.7 °C by 2025, without resetting the spatial pattern. Because this wet anomaly confounds interpretation as a continuous trend, the 2015–2025 comparison was treated as an interannual snapshot comparison rather than a linear trend analysis. Standard deviation ellipse (SDE) analysis revealed a net southeastward shift of the heat island centroid (~ 0.72 km). NDBBI showed the strongest positive correlation with LST ( r = 0.86) and FVC the strongest negative correlation ( r = − 0.77). Spatial principal component analysis (SPCA) extracted three composite drivers explaining 77.2% of variance. A tentative comparison of summed regression coefficients suggested a larger aggregate association for human-related factors than natural factors, though these are associations, not causal estimates. These findings highlight the need for targeted interventions for Nairobi’s approximately 2.5 million informal settlement residents. header: Mapping educational infrastructure for rapid urban growth through analysis of spatial inequality and school siting priorities in Adama city, Ethiopia | Discover Cities | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Discover Cities Article Mapping educational infrastructure for rapid urban growth through analysis of spatial inequality and school siting priorities in Adama city, Ethiopia Research Open access Published: 06 November 2026 Volume 3 , article number 223 ( 2026 ) Cite this article You have full access to this open access article Download PDF Save article View saved research Discover Cities Aims and scope Submit manuscript Mapping educational infrastructure for rapid urban growth through analysis of spatial inequality and school siting priorities in Adama city, Ethiopia Download PDF Elshadai Baja Woldetsadik ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-0672-9671 1 , 2 & Dejene Tesema Bulti 3 Abstract Rapid peri-urban growth in Global South secondary cities consistently outpaces municipal public service delivery, generating severe spatial inequalities. This paper examines the spatial and institutional production of primary school infrastructure deficits in Adama City, Ethiopia. Deploying a mixed-method approach, this study integrates a GIS-based Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) site suitability model configured at a precise 30 m \(\:\times\:\) 30 m grid resolution, a 384-household socioeconomic survey, 12 key informant interviews with planning and education officials, and four focus group discussions with community leaders, parents, and teachers. The spatial model indicates that while 16.14% of municipal land is highly suitable for educational infrastructure, existing school infrastructure remains concentrated in saturated central cores rather than in these newly identified peripheral priority zones. This spatial mismatch coincides with severe overcrowding: the 12 schools identified as operating above capacity average 58 students per classroom. Analytically, spatial and field validation indicated that 73% of the area classified as underserved (by household, administrative, and stakeholder indicators) fell within model-identified high-suitability zones; because the validation indicators and the model criteria draw on related conditions, this is evidence of convergence rather than fully independent validation. Qualitative findings suggest that accessibility deficits are shaped not merely by geographic friction, but also by institutional land-reservation failures, unauthorized land-use conversions, and un-synchronized capital investment cycles. This study contributes by indicating how spatial decision-support tools may need to be coupled with institutional governance reforms to enforce land-use zoning and mitigate infrastructure lag in rapidly expanding secondary cities. For Adama and comparable Global South secondary cities, the findings suggest that GIS-AHP suitability outputs should be embedded within binding land-reservation and inter-agency coordination mechanisms before, rather than after, peripheral settlement occurs. header: A comparative study of domestic gardening across socioeconomic and housing contexts in two urban communities in Greater Accra, Ghana | Discover Cities | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Discover Cities Article A comparative study of domestic gardening across socioeconomic and housing contexts in two urban communities in Greater Accra, Ghana Research Open access Published: 06 November 2026 Volume 3 , article number 222 ( 2026 ) Cite this article You have full access to this open access article Download PDF Save article View saved research Discover Cities Aims and scope Submit manuscript A comparative study of domestic gardening across socioeconomic and housing contexts in two urban communities in Greater Accra, Ghana Download PDF Henry Mensah 1 , Samuel Boamah Asiedu 2 , Dorothy Julian Nalumu 3 , David Langnel 4 , Eric Kwame Simpeh 1 , Patrick Opoku 5 & … Eric Oduro-Ofori 6 Show authors 178 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract This study examines the potential of domestic gardens to support urban sustainability in Greater Accra, Ghana. It explores homeowners’ perceptions of the social, economic, and ecological benefits of domestic gardening and identifies the main factors influencing engagement across two socioeconomically distinct communities, East Legon and Kwabenya. A comparative quantitative survey design, complemented by illustrative field observations, was used to collect data from 226 household heads through structured questionnaires. The Mann–Whitney U test was used to examine differences in perceptions between the two communities, while the Relative Importance Index (RII) was used to rank the perceived ecological, personal, and economic drivers of domestic gardening. The results indicate significant differences between the two communities in perceptions of healthy eating ( r = 0.804), poverty reduction ( r = 0.490), and sustainable technology adoption ( r = 0.316). Despite these differences, homeowners in both communities recognized several important ecological functions of domestic gardening, particularly microclimate regulation, flood mitigation, and soil enrichment. Field observations further illustrate differences in gardening practices, ranging from ornamental and technology-supported gardens in East Legon to more food-oriented gardens in Kwabenya. The findings highlight domestic gardens as important socio-ecological assets in sub-Saharan African (SSA) cities and provide evidence for incorporating private residential green spaces into broader urban sustainability and climate adaptation strategies. header: Pluvial flood impacts on ambulance travel and spatial disparities in emergency healthcare accessibility in Thessaloniki, Greece | Discover Cities | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Discover Cities Article Pluvial flood impacts on ambulance travel and spatial disparities in emergency healthcare accessibility in Thessaloniki, Greece Research Open access Published: 05 November 2026 Volume 3 , article number 221 ( 2026 ) Cite this article You have full access to this open access article Download PDF Save article View saved research Discover Cities Aims and scope Submit manuscript Pluvial flood impacts on ambulance travel and spatial disparities in emergency healthcare accessibility in Thessaloniki, Greece Download PDF Dimos Touloumidis ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-0652-7028 1 , 2 , Michael Madas ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-9809-8485 1 , Christos Iliadis ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-1181-3686 3 , 4 , Sofoklis Dais ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-5219-0315 2 & … Vassilis Glenis ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-6037-9508 3 Show authors 40 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract Urban pluvial flooding can disrupt road networks, delay emergency medical services and produce spatially uneven losses of access to urgent healthcare. This study evaluates how flood-induced road disruption affects ambulance travel performance and identifies buildings, neighbourhoods and populations that experience reduced emergency healthcare accessibility under rainfall events with return periods of 10, 20 and 100 years in Thessaloniki, Greece. High-resolution flood-depth outputs were integrated with direction-specific road operating speeds, building footprints, population estimates, an ambulance terminal and seven public hospitals. Road-section speeds were adjusted according to local flood depth and impassable sections were removed, while minimum-time routes were then calculated for the terminal-to-patient, patient-to-hospital and hospital-to-terminal legs across 21 two-hospital duty configurations. Flooding produced substantial increases in travel time and distance even though only a small proportion of road links became impassable. Under the 100-year scenario, the median full-service-cycle time increased from 24.8 to 33.0 min, patient-delivery completion declined from 100.0% to 86.1% and the proportion of journeys completed within 30 min fell from 97.3% to 56.1%. The patient-to-hospital leg deteriorated most, while comparison with baseline revealed that the greatest flood-related reductions in patient-delivery accessibility within 30 min occurred in northern and northwestern Thessaloniki under the modelled terminal and hospital-duty configurations. The study provides an integrated framework that combines ambulance travel modelling with building- and population-level accessibility analysis under flood conditions. The findings show that limited but strategically located road disruptions can generate disproportionate operational and spatial impacts, highlighting the importance of protecting critical corridors, supporting flood-aware routing and considering hospital availability in emergency preparedness planning. header: National innovation capacity and the decoupling of economic growth from carbon emissions evidence from dynamic panel analysis | Discover Environment | Springer Nature Link Skip to main content Advertisement Log in Menu Find a journal Publish with us Track your research Search Saved research Cart Home Discover Environment Article National innovation capacity and the decoupling of economic growth from carbon emissions evidence from dynamic panel analysis Research Open access Published: 06 November 2026 Volume 4 , article number 636 ( 2026 ) Cite this article You have full access to this open access article Download PDF Save article View saved research Discover Environment Aims and scope Submit manuscript National innovation capacity and the decoupling of economic growth from carbon emissions evidence from dynamic panel analysis Download PDF Benedict Afful Jr. ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0002-7461-2275 1 & Kassim Alabani ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-0262-9366 1 Abstract Focusing on Sub-Saharan Africa, this research examines whether national innovation capacity drives the decoupling of economic growth from CO₂ emissions and how institutional quality moderates this link. Using a panel of 47 Sub-Saharan African countries over the period 2005–2024, the study constructs a residual-based CO₂–GDP decoupling index and applies two-way fixed-effects estimation, dynamic two-step System Generalized Method of Moments (System GMM), and Method of Moments Quantile Regression (MM-QR) to address unobserved heterogeneity, endogeneity, dynamic persistence, and distributional heterogeneity. The results show that national innovation capacity and institutional quality are positively and statistically associated with CO₂–GDP decoupling in the fixed-effects and MM-QR estimations, with the positive effects observed across lower, median, and upper conditional quantiles of the decoupling distribution. In contrast, neither effect is statistically significant in the short-run dynamic System GMM specifications, suggesting that the contribution of innovation and institutional quality to decoupling operates primarily through gradual structural adjustments rather than immediate changes in emissions intensity. Globalization is consistently associated with weaker decoupling, and its adverse effect becomes larger at higher conditional quantiles. Continuous time-interaction estimates further show that the marginal effect of national innovation capacity on decoupling strengthens progressively over the sample period, indicating a growing contribution of innovation to the separation of economic growth from CO₂ emissions. The findings suggest that innovation capacity alone may not be sufficient to achieve sustained growth–emissions decoupling. Effective decarbonization requires technological upgrading to be supported by stronger institutions, financial allocation toward low-carbon activities, and trade and external economic policies that limit the transmission of carbon-intensive production and investment. The study concludes that Innovation alone is insufficient to guarantee stronger decoupling; it must be institutionally enabled, financially directed, and environmentally targeted. Abstract Standard setters have increased their commitments to ensuring more standardized and high-quality information as the need to address climate change evolves. Abstract This study examines the relationship between women's labour force participation and Economic Growth in Somalia, a fragile economy characterized by high informality and persistent gender disparities. This paper proposes a Procedural Learning Framework to support the co-creation of sponge measures and strategies across spatial levels. It was developed through a scoping review of process-oriented implementation frameworks and action-oriented research with stakeholder knowledge in the Horizon Europe Innovation Action project SpongeWorks. While maintaining high recharge potential theoretically supports subsurface water storage and landscape resilience against extreme weather events, long-term spatial evaluations of how land-use policies preserve these functions remain limited. Despite the abundance of water resources in Brazil, insufficient coordination between land-use planning and groundwater management compromises water security. There is a knowledge gap regarding long-term spatial-temporal evaluations of how territorial policies, rather than land use alone, affect the maintenance of groundwater recharge potential. This study addresses this gap by assessing the impact of territorial policies on aquifer recharge potential over time. The purpose of this paper is to demonstrate the need for territorial policies governing freshwater management to support long-term water security. This study examined a volcanic plateau in southern Brazil to illustrate a framework. Using a GIS approach, this paper established a method for evaluating GWRPZ changes between 1985 and 2022 and compared these changes with territories under different land-use restrictions. The resulting GWRPZ change map showed areas where recharge potential had improved and others where it had been reduced between 1985 and 2022. Higher GWRPZ maintenance was associated with a higher degree of area protection. Agriculture was identified as the main pressure on GWRPZs, whereas the main resistance was forest recovery. These data can help inform policy decision-making to identify more applicable and appropriate solutions for sustainable development. Multiple stressors contribute to soil pollution, including the use of plant protection products (here: pesticides). Policy goals, however, demand that the EU and Germany protect biodiversity and soils. Against this background, the present article adopts a qualitative governance analysis to investigate the extent to which German pesticide policies contribute to reduced pesticide pollution risks as well as biodiversity and soil health goals. Results indicate that (1) pesticide use requirements have a very limited steering effect on reducing pesticide pollution risks because they lack precision and enforceability, (2) pesticide spatial measures suffer from enforcement and control issues, an extensive exception regime and poorly implemented restrictions. Still, certain policy elements such as training and certification, as well as the expansion of water protection areas contribute to some extent to reduced pesticide pollution risks, biodiversity and soil health. These results indicate that effective soil protection not only requires incremental changes in existing policies but comprehensive amendments to the agricultural sector including the adoption of economic instruments and measures from the global to the local level. Gutiérrez-Jurado 2 , 6 Show authors 709 Accesses Explore all metrics Abstract Agricultural sustainability in closed endorheic basins is constrained by periodic water scarcity, hydrological isolation, and the cumulative effects of intensive land use. The Cuauhtémoc region of northern Mexico hosts long-established Mennonite farming communities whose mechanized and irrigation-dependent agriculture constitutes an important component of the regional economy and resource-use system. This study examined the prevalence, diversity, and drivers of sustainable agricultural practices among 95 Mennonite farmers in the Bustillos Lagoon region. Thirteen practices spanning soil and residue management, water conservation, biological soil-fertility management, and agrochemical stewardship were assessed, while a conservation-practice breadth indicator quantified the number of ten resource-management practices used by individual farmers. Among 92 farmers with complete practice data, conservation-practice breadth ranged from 2 to 8 practices (mean = 3.76 ± 1.06). Residue incorporation (98.9%), residue cover (89.4%), and rainwater collection (71.0%) were widespread, whereas zero tillage (1.1%), compost/leachate use (5.3%), mycorrhiza application (5.3%), and reduced tillage (8.5%) were uncommon. Robust Poisson regression showed that technical assistance was associated with a 37.8% higher expected conservation-practice count (IRR = 1.378, 95% CI 1.168-1.626, p < 0.001), while environmental concern was associated with an 18.7% higher count (IRR = 1.187, 95% CI 1.017-1.385, p = 0.030). Water-supply problems, farm area, producer-organization membership, and education showed no independent associations. The findings demonstrate that sustainable management is better characterized as a heterogeneous portfolio of practices than as a binary adoption decision and highlight institutional support and environmental orientation as important correlates of management diversification in water-constrained agricultural landscapes.
